title: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors
one_liner: A neutral calculation agent runs a county-approved, developer-funded home-value guarantee for houses near proposed data centers, using pre-announcement baselines and public sale records with no sensors, and unspent escrow reverts to the developer, which makes it cheaper than $10k checks and more credible.
customer: Payer: independent data center developers and their CFOs and general counsel, especially those that have already tried lump-sum checks or buyouts and got 'bribe' coverage (NorthPoint-type offers, Mason County-type buyouts). Co-signer: county commissions that put the guarantee into a development agreement. Distribution partners: title and escrow companies, mortgage lenders and local realtors in the impact radius, who deliver claims at the point of sale. Beneficiaries: owner-occupants within roughly 1-3 miles.
problem: Residents' biggest fear is not a sensor reading, it is the value of their house. Developers are already spending on this fear in the worst way: NorthPoint's $10k-per-household offer ($45M across 4,500 households) was called a bribe, and Propmodo expects future offers to move to 'utility bill credits or property value guarantees rather than lump sums'. A check pays 100% of households for a risk that only touches the minority who sell at a loss, buys no trust, and leaves the price question unresolved. Home-value anecdotes are contested (a 4-bedroom listed 15-18% lower next to a Northern Virginia hyperscale site; the NAR 2026 Data Center Impact Report and local reporting disagree on how far effects reach), so both sides are arguing about a number nobody has pre-agreed.
solution: Product: a Property Value Assurance Program administered as a contract, not insurance. The developer is the obligor and funds an escrow (illustratively $3-5k per eligible household, against $10k of certain checks) with a corporate escrow agent at signing of the development agreement. We are the neutral calculation agent, the way a calculation agent works in a structured contract. Mechanics: (1) Freeze a reference value for each enrolled home at the date of first public disclosure of the project, using an AVM plus a broker price opinion (about $300), with a full appraisal only if disputed. (2) Publish a county-wide control index (repeat-sales or hedonic, plus matched control neighborhoods) so market moves are separated from project effects. (3) If the owner sells at arm's length within 10 years (listed 60+ days, arm's-length buyer), we pay from escrow the shortfall between the net sale price and the control-index-adjusted reference value, up to a cap (for example 20% of reference). (4) Unspent escrow reverts to the developer at year 10, or is split with a community fund. (5) No sensors: the trigger is a price versus a pre-agreed formula, so there is no argument about causation, only about arithmetic. Adverse selection and gaming are handled with the arm's-length rule, an exposure cap and a three-appraiser tie-break (already the norm in Mason County buyouts).
why_now: In 2026 lump-sum neighbor payments went mainstream and drew immediate backlash (NorthPoint, September 2026 coverage), while moratoria in NY (July 14) and Texas (Sept 21) plus local pauses give developers a reason to look for a structure that survives a hearing. Data-center adjacency is now a mainstream real-estate question: Realtor.com counts 108 ZIP codes with a large data center by June 2026, up from 12 in 2015, and NAR and HousingWire are publishing on it, so buyers and lenders already ask. AVMs, MLS and deed data are cheap and standardized. Wind developers have used property-value guarantees as permit conditions, so counties and lawyers recognize the form.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer from the program budget. Illustrative 3,000-household program: $300 per household enrollment (AVM, BPO, lien check, portal) = $900k; 1% per year of a $12M escrow = $120k; $1,500 per adjudicated sale claim; optional 50 bps share of escrow yield (T-bill yield on $12M is meaningful float for the agent-of-record bank to share). Roughly $1M+ of year-one revenue per program, about 10x the parent's $75-150k sensor setup, with software-like margins after the model is built. Second revenue line: sell the control-index and price-effect research to counties, lenders and appraisers. Assumptions to test: 10-25% of homes sell within 10 years and only some at a shortfall; expected payout 10-30% of escrow.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is cheaper for the developer than a check and more persuasive to the neighbor, at the same time: the expected payout is only the shortfall on homes that actually sell at a loss, and unspent money returns, while residents receive the thing they said they wanted (protection of value, per Propmodo) instead of hush money. It also sidesteps the attribution trap that hurts the parent, because the trigger is a formula on public deed data, not a causal claim about a well or a hum. And it aligns incentives: every year the facility runs quietly is a year the developer's escrow is not drawn, so neighbors and developer want the same outcome. Making the developer the obligor also removes the insurance-law problem the parent's escrow payout faced.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the price-effect model on deed and MLS data around 3 existing clusters (for example Loudoun and Prince William VA and one Georgia or Texas site) using difference-in-differences against matched control neighborhoods, and publish 'what data centers actually do to nearby home prices' (this is both lead generation and the expected-payout estimate). Days 10-20: write a 2-page term sheet and a development-agreement rider; call the government-relations and general-counsel offices of 8-10 independent developers that have publicly offered checks, buyouts or community funds. Days 15-30: pitch two county attorneys with pending hearings; line up a corporate escrow agent and one title company. Target: a letter of intent for a 300-household pilot with a $1M escrow. Gate at 90 days: one signed pilot or one county condition, plus a counsel view that the developer-obligor structure is not insurance in that state.
lineage: mutation of I1172 ('Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring), Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis), Envirosuite (ASX:EVS), Kunak. White space: Nobody found sells the bundle, so the status is 'gap' and not 'open'. The sensor and baseline layer is not open: KETOS (about $45M raised) pitches an independent baseline for data centers, Aethair pitches pre-construction baselines, Envirosuite has community dashboards, and consultancies bundle baselines into permitting. The unserved wedge is what sits on top of the sensors. (1) A neutral administrator holding escrowed, tamper-evident data whose governance the county and community accept, unlike developer-hired consultants and unlike opposition-side groups such as CEDS. (2) The Neighbor Guarantee: an automatic, no-litigation payout to households from a developer-funded escrow when a pre-agreed trigger is hit. No vendor, insurer, county ordinance or developer program found does this. The nearest things are Franklin County, Indiana's draft rule (escrow for 24-hour emergency potable water to impacted neighbors, plus developer-funded monitoring wells), one-off buyouts and lump-sum checks. (3) A 10-year, multi-parameter (wells, noise, PM2.5, voltage) record packaged as a permit-condition template that regulators can adopt. Weak points: the sensor baseline will commoditize; attribution is hard, because well drawdown from drought or other pumping is indistinguishable from data-center drawdown unless the design uses upgradient control wells and pumping records; automatic payouts may look like insurance under state law; and developer counsel may resist a pre-committed payout as an admission of liability. Note: the web-search budget ran out before I could check Crunchbase/YC directly for a startup doing exactly the escrow-plus-parametric bundle, so 'nobody found' means no evidence in about 25 searches, not proof of absence. | How this version avoids them: KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, Kunak, Clarity, Larson Davis and Eno are all sensor or environmental-data vendors and none touches property value, so there is no overlap in product, buyer budget line or moat. Consultancies (TRC, Salas O'Brien) sell permitting studies, not a financial guarantee administered after approval. Prevolt and Jambo sell risk screens and engagement software, not a payout mechanism. CEDS is an opposition-side advisory group. The developer-run substitutes (NorthPoint checks, Mason County buyouts, Microsoft's Community-First pledge) are the budget we redirect, and they lack a neutral administrator and a pre-agreed formula. A web check found no productized, third-party-administered data-center property-value guarantee (wind-project guarantees are bespoke and appraiser-run); verify in week 1. Title and escrow firms could copy the mechanics but lack model neutrality and county-approved governance.

competitors.name: KETOS (SHIELD / KELP data-center water monitoring)
competitors.what_they_do: Continuous water-quality monitoring plus chain-of-custody lab testing. Their data-center page pitches 'the missing baseline': independent measurement at wells, outfalls and streams before and after a facility is built. Buyers named are operators, utilities and residents. Testing packages start at $469. No neighbor payout or escrow guarantee.
competitors.scale_or_funding: About $44.8M raised over 9 rounds (Crunchbase/CB Insights via search); latest $10M round led by Tenfore Holdings (https://igrownews.com/ketos-secures-10-million-in-funding/)

competitors.name: Aethair (Aethair PRO, Environet, Thiamis)
competitors.what_they_do: Air-quality and noise monitoring hardware plus dashboards. They publish a data-center guide that recommends 'a baseline before construction starts' and address both operators and communities. Their platform can also ingest third-party water sensors. No guarantee or escrow product.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Operating since 2017 in 45+ countries; reported as unfunded (PitchBook/Tracxn snippets: https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/267793-66)

competitors.name: Envirosuite (ASX:EVS)
competitors.what_they_do: Listed environmental-monitoring SaaS for airports, mines, ports and industrial sites. Offers community-facing public noise and air dashboards and resident complaint intake. Its air monitors are powered by Kunak. This is the strongest incumbent that could add a data-center 'community trust' package.

competitors.name: Kunak
competitors.what_they_do: Outdoor air-quality sensor stations. Virginia DEQ placed five Kunak/APEX sensors in Loudoun 'data center alley' in Feb 2026, so this is a public-sector baseline already running.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established hardware vendor; supplies Envirosuite and Virginia DEQ (https://www.deq.virginia.gov/news-info/shortcuts/topics-of-interest/data-center-air-monitoring-project)

competitors.name: Clarity
competitors.what_they_do: Low-cost networked air-quality nodes and a data-center air monitoring guide. Sells to municipalities, consultants and NGOs. No payout mechanism.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established venture-backed sensor company (funding not verified)

competitors.name: Larson Davis and Soundtrace (acoustic monitoring)
competitors.what_they_do: Professional noise-monitoring instruments and cloud compliance dashboards marketed to data centers. Soundtrace: https://www.soundtrace.com/blog/data-center-noise-monitoring-osha-compliance-guide. Commodity hardware the idea would buy, or that a consultant could bundle.

competitors.name: CEDS (Community & Environmental Defense Services)
competitors.what_they_do: Non-profit that helps residents design citizen monitoring programs (noise, PurpleAir PM2.5, USGS well data) and advises that pre-construction, construction and post-construction baselines be collected. It sits on the opposition side, so it is not a neutral steward. It also says applicants should fund expert and drilling costs via payments to local government.

competitors.name: Engineering and environmental consultancies (TRC, Salas O'Brien, Trinity, SCS)
competitors.what_they_do: Already sell developers baseline noise, air and hydrogeology studies as part of permitting. Salas O'Brien: https://salasobrien.com/news/data-centers-acoustics-environmental-noise-control/. They are the default vendor for the baseline layer, but they are developer-hired and therefore not trusted as neutral.

competitors.name: Prevolt and Jambo (developer-side community-risk software)
competitors.what_they_do: Prevolt sells community and political risk screens to infrastructure and data-center developers. Jambo sells stakeholder-relationship software for data-center community engagement (https://www.jambo.cloud/blog/build-data-center-community-support-before-public). Neither does monitoring or guarantees. They compete for the same 'social license' budget line.

competitors.name: Developer-run substitutes: NorthPoint $10k checks, Mason County 'Good Neighbors' buyout, Microsoft Community-First pledge
competitors.what_they_do: Developers already spend directly on neighbors, with no neutral administrator and no evidence layer. Buyout: https://wchstv.com/news/local/voluntary-buyout-offers-rolled-out-for-meadowlands-estates-homes-near-data-center. Microsoft: https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2026/01/13/community-first-ai-infrastructure/. Residents call the lump sums a 'bribe'. This is the budget the idea would redirect, and it is not a competing product.
competitors.scale_or_funding: NorthPoint offer: $45M across 4,500 households; Microsoft: $25M+ for Virginia water and sewer upgrades

competitors.name: Eno Scientific and ParemTech (well-level sensors)
competitors.what_they_do: Off-the-shelf well water-level loggers for homeowners, agriculture and municipalities. No data-center product. This is commodity hardware for the well-monitoring node, and it lowers the barrier for anyone copying the sensor layer.

I1172.evidence_of_demand:
Strong on policy pull and on the problem, thin on proof anyone pays for the exact bundle.
- Regulators are writing developer-funded independent monitoring into rules. Franklin County, IN draft ordinance: developer-paid real-time monitoring wells, a licensed-hydrogeologist impact assessment, and an escrow for 24-hour potable water to impacted neighbors (https://www.franklincounty.in.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Data-Center-Regulations-Draft-v3.0-03.30.26-1.pdf and https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8103901/indiana/franklin-county/franklin-county-workgroup-seeks-strict-water-protections-for-proposed-data-centers). Shenandoah County, VA officials back independent third-party testing funded by the applicant (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9504403/virginia/shenandoah-county/officials-ask-stronger-noise-air-quality-monitoring-and-enforcement-for-future-data-centers). St. Louis's permit requires an annual third-party noise report and a developer-funded hydraulic model study (https://www.stlouis-mo.gov/government/departments/mayor/news/data-center-permit-approved.cfm).
- A live baseline-less dispute: Meta's Newton County, GA neighbors say their wells went dry or silted up. Meta's own study says groundwater flows away from them, and families sued in Sept 2026 (https://www.ajc.com/news/2026/09/georgia-families-sue-meta-accuse-its-data-center-of-tainting-their-water/, https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2025/07/15/meta-built-a-new-data-center-in-georgia-their-neighbors-water-ran-dry/). This shows developer-commissioned studies are not believed. Cheyenne's Meta-contractor wastewater contamination led to a $10k fine (https://fortune.com/2026/07/10/wyoming-officials-meta-715000-square-foot-data-center-responsible-contaminating-water-system-rare-bacterium/).
- Developers are already spending on neighbors with no neutral mechanism, and residents reject it. NorthPoint's $10k-per-household offer ($45M) was called a bribe, with residents wanting property-value protection instead (https://reason.com/2026/09/28/data-centers-and-their-discontents/, https://propmodo.com/cash-to-residents-is-the-newest-tool-in-the-data-center-fight/). Propmodo expects future versions to be 'tied to utility bill credits or property value guarantees rather than lump sums'. The Mason County developer offers buyouts at the highest of three independent valuations plus a premium, with no independent oversight (https://wchstv.com/news/local/voluntary-buyout-offers-rolled-out-for-meadowlands-estates-homes-near-data-center).
- Precedent that baseline mandates create a paid vendor category: Pennsylvania Act 13 (oil and gas) makes operators pay third-party pre-drill water tests for wells within 1,000 ft, and a rebuttable presumption of liability applies when no baseline exists (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/programs-and-services/oil-and-gas/related-topics/act-13/act-13-faq). No equivalent presumption exists yet for data centers, so developers currently lack a legal reason to buy.
- The 'why now' facts check out. NY Executive Order 62, July 14, 2026, pauses DEC discretionary permits for 50 MW+ data centers (https://www.dwt.com/blogs/energy--environmental-law-blog/2026/07/ny-data-center-permitting-pause-executive-order-62). Texas ordered TCEQ to halt data-center permits on Sept 21, 2026 (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/21/texas-governor-abbott-ai-data-center-permits.html). Reuters/Ipsos: 14% comfortable with a data center nearby, 57% opposed (https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2026-06-11/americans-wary-of-ai-driven-data-center-boom-reuters-ipsos-poll-shows). I could not verify the 'local pauses in at least 14 states' claim.
- Vendor signals (marketing, not proof of spend): KETOS's 'missing baseline' pitch (https://ketos.co/data-centers-water-quality) and a groundwater-marketing blog saying monitoring and hydrogeology services are 'being specified in RFPs right now' (https://groundwatermarketing.com/blog/data-centers-groundwater-demand/).
- Not found: any developer or county publicly paying a neutral party for a parametric neighbor payout, or any RFP for one.
I1172.sharper_angle:
Do not sell 'Baseline-in-a-Box' as a sensor product, because KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite and the developer-hired consultancies already cover it and it will commoditize. Sell neutral trusteeship of a neighbor-protection covenant, starting with well water only.

1. Be the escrow and trust administrator plus an independent technical panel, with governance the county co-approves. Buy commodity sensors and labs from KETOS, Kunak or Eno Scientific-type vendors instead of competing with them.
2. Lead with a well-drawdown guarantee, because dry or silted wells drive the lawsuits and hearings (Meta Newton County). Fix the attribution problem in the trigger design. Use upgradient control wells, pumping records and a difference-versus-control test, so the developer pays only for excess drawdown and not for drought. Bring in an MGA or carrier partner for capacity so the payout is legally clean and does not run into state insurance law.
3. Sell it to counties as a ready-made permit-condition and development-agreement template, aimed first at jurisdictions already drafting escrow-for-neighbors language (Franklin County, IN; Shenandoah, VA). The county mandates it, the developer funds it, and you skip the developer's reluctance to volunteer a payout.
4. Add noise, PM2.5 and voltage as paid extensions later. Enroll per household instead of pricing bespoke $75-150k builds.

First proof to get: one county or developer willing to put the guarantee escrow in writing, and a counsel opinion on whether the structure is insurance. If neither exists within about 90 days, the idea collapses into the crowded monitoring market and should be dropped.
